claim: CIDEA is a lipid droplet protein enriched in brown adipocytes.
source: CIDEA is a lipid droplet (LD)-protein enriched in brown adipocytes promoting the enlargement of LDs, which are dynamic, ubiquitous organelles specialized for storing neutral lipids.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of CIDEA.

claim: CIDEA promotes the enlargement of lipid droplets.
source: CIDEA is a lipid droplet (LD)-protein enriched in brown adipocytes promoting the enlargement of LDs, which are dynamic, ubiquitous organelles specialized for storing neutral lipids.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: CIDEA contains an amphipathic helix that facilitates embedding in the LD phospholipid monolayer.
source: We demonstrate an essential role in this process for an amphipathic helix in CIDEA, which facilitates embedding in the LD phospholipid monolayer and binds phosphatidic acid (PA).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CD spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations in the results.

claim: The amphipathic helix in CIDEA binds phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: We demonstrate an essential role in this process for an amphipathic helix in CIDEA, which facilitates embedding in the LD phospholipid monolayer and binds phosphatidic acid (PA).
evidence: This is demonstrated through lipid strip assays, PA bead binding assays, and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: LD pairs are docked by CIDEA trans-complexes through contributions of the N-terminal domain and a C-terminal dimerization region.
source: LD pairs are docked by CIDEA trans-complexes through contributions of the N-terminal domain and a C-terminal dimerization region.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and mutational analysis showing both N-term and C-term regions contribute to LD-LD docking.

claim: CIDEA complexes are enriched at the LD-LD contact site.
source: These complexes, enriched at the LD–LD contact site, interact with the cone-shaped phospholipid PA and likely increase phospholipid barrier permeability, promoting LD fusion by transference of lipids.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1C.

claim: CIDEA interaction with PA increases phospholipid barrier permeability to promote LD fusion by lipid transference.
source: These complexes, enriched at the LD–LD contact site, interact with the cone-shaped phospholipid PA and likely increase phospholipid barrier permeability, promoting LD fusion by transference of lipids.
evidence: This is supported by PA depletion experiments in yeast and mammalian cells, and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: During differentiation of immortalized brown pre-adipocytes, large LDs are formed by the fusion of pre-existing LDs.
source: During differentiation of immortalized brown pre-adipocytes, large LDs were formed by the fusion of pre-existing LDs (Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse microscopy shown in Video 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: LD fusion during brown adipocyte differentiation is characterized by slow and progressive reduction in the volume of a donor LD until it is completely absorbed by an acceptor LD.
source: This fusion process was characterized by a slow and progressive reduction in the volume of a donor LD until it was completely absorbed by an acceptor LD (Figure 1A), which is characteristic of CIDE activity.
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The LD fusion pattern observed during brown adipocyte differentiation is characteristic of CIDE activity.
source: This fusion process was characterized by a slow and progressive reduction in the volume of a donor LD until it was completely absorbed by an acceptor LD (Figure 1A), which is characteristic of CIDE activity.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known CIDE protein behavior from literature.

claim: CIDEA is selectively expressed in brown adipocytes.
source: As CIDEA is selectively expressed in brown adipocytes and could have a prominent role in the acquisition of their multilocular morphology, we explored the effects of its expression in undifferentiated pre-adipocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction and results sections.

claim: After inducing CIDEA expression, LDs in pre-adipocytes show progressive fusion of initial LDs until a few large LDs remain in the cell.
source: After inducing CIDEA, LDs in pre-adipocytes showed an equivalent dynamic pattern to that observed in differentiating brown cells, with the progressive fusion of the initial LDs until a few large LDs remained in the cell (Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse microscopy shown in Video 2 and Figure 1B.

claim: LD fusion induced by CIDEA is preceded by the formation of small clusters of interacting LDs.
source: LD fusion was achieved by the slow transference of lipids between LDs, and was preceded by the formation of small clusters of interacting LDs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: The ectopic expression of full-length CIDEA induces the formation of large LDs through LD fusion by lipid transfer.
source: The ectopic expression of full-length CIDEA induced the formation of large LDs through LD fusion by lipid transfer (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence and time-lapse imaging in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Control cells lacking CIDEA expression do not show LD enlargement.
source: Control cells, which lacked expression of CIDEA, did not show LD enlargement (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown through comparison with control cells in Figure 1C.

claim: CIDEA contains four highly conserved regions when compared with CIDEB and CIDEC.
source: By comparing the 217 amino acid (aa) sequence of CIDEA with that of CIDEB and CIDEC, four highly conserved regions could be identified (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through sequence alignment analysis in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CIDEA is composed of a basic region (2-72 aa) followed by an acidic sequence (73-110 aa).
source: The N-terminal (N-term) domain of CIDEA is composed of a basic region (2–72 aa) followed by an acidic sequence (73–110 aa).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The distinctly differently charged regions in the N-terminal domain are important for the dimerization of CIDE domain proteins according to protein crystallography studies.
source: These distinctly differently charged regions are indicated by protein crystallography studies to be important for the dimerization of CIDE domain proteins (Lugovskoy et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystallography studies.

claim: The CIDEA C-terminal is rich in basic amino acids and contains a highly conserved region (126-155 aa) and a basic and hydrophobic sequence (162-197 aa).
source: The CIDEA C-terminal (C-term) is rich in basic aas and contains a highly conserved region (126–155 aa) and a basic and hydrophobic sequence (162–197 aa).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The molecular mechanism of CIDEA is composed of three discrete phases: LD targeting, LD-LD docking, and LD growth.
source: Together with the time-lapse results, this indicates that the molecular mechanism of CIDEA is composed of three discrete phases: LD targeting, LD–LD docking, and LD growth.
evidence: This is inferred from mutational analysis showing different mutations affect different steps of the process.

claim: The R171E/R175E mutation in CIDEA promotes aggregation of cellular LDs in 'bunch of grapes'-like LD clusters but is unable to induce lipid transference between them.
source: Interestingly, certain mutations such as R171E/R175E promoted the aggregation of the cellular LDs in a few 'bunch of grapes'-like LD clusters, but were unable to induce the transference of lipids between them (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging and phenotypic analysis in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: CIDEA-(116-217)-v5 expression results in LDs remaining small and dispersed throughout the cytoplasm despite the protein being normally localized at their surface.
source: In other cases, as with the expression of CIDEA-(116–217)-v5, the LDs remained small and dispersed throughout the cytoplasm despite the protein being normally localized at their surface.
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C and imaging in Figure 4A.

claim: CIDEA-(1-118)-v5 shows no LD localization and does not affect LD size, number, or distribution.
source: Finally, some versions of CIDEA, such as CIDEA-(1–118)-v5, showed no LD localization and did not affect their size, number, or distribution.
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: All CIDEA constructs that showed impaired LD localization contained deletions or mutations in the C-term hydrophobic and basic region (162-197 aa).
source: All the CIDEA constructs that showed impaired LD localization contained deletions or mutations in the C-term hydrophobic and basic region (162–197 aa) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The last 66 amino acids of CIDEA are sufficient for LD localization.
source: In fact, the last 66 aas of CIDEA were sufficient for LD localization, as shown with the expression of CIDEA-(152–217)-v5, whereas it lacked the ability to facilitate the docking of LDs (Figures 2C and 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4A and phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The C-term domain of CIDE proteins is essential for LD localization and enlargement.
source: Although it is known that the C-term domain of CIDE proteins is essential for LD localization and enlargement (Liu et al., 2009; Christianson et al., 2010), only the structure of the N-term domain has been solved (Lugovskoy et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The CIDE-N domain has been determined in members of the CIDE family to amino acids 40-117, 34-100, and 41-118 in hCIDEA, hCIDEB, and mCIDEC, respectively.
source: The CIDE-N domain (Pfam reference PF02017) has been determined in members of the CIDE family (PBD Codes: 2eel (hCIDEA), 1D4B (hCIDEB), 4MAC (mCIDEC), 4ikg (mCIDEC)) to aas 40–117, 34–100, and 41–118 in hCIDEA, hCIDEB, and mCIDEC, respectively.
evidence: This is based on structural data from protein databases.

claim: The sequence 163-180 in CIDEA lacks direct structural information.
source: Thus, the sequence 163–180 that we found essential for LD targeting (Figure 2C) lacks direct structural information to date.
evidence: This is stated based on lack of available structural data.

claim: The region 163-180 in CIDEA displays high probability of a helical conformation with a strongly amphipathic character.
source: The region displayed high probability of a helical conformation with a strongly amphipathic character (Figure 3A,B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through computational structure prediction in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Circular dichroism spectroscopy confirmed the presence of an amphipathic helix in the LD-targeting domain of CIDEA.
source: To experimentally confirm the presence of an amphipathic helix in the LD-targeting domain of CIDEA, circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy was used to estimate the secondary structure of a synthetic peptide corresponding to residues 158–185 in CIDEA. The CD spectra in the presence of 0.1% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside confirmed the presence of α-helical structure (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HA-CIDEA-(1-117)-(163-180) is partially localized on the LD surface and promotes LD clustering.
source: While HA-(1–120)-CIDEA showed no LD localization and had no effect on LD distribution or size, HA-CIDEA-(1–117)-(163–180) was partially localized on the LD surface and promoted LD clustering (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3D.

claim: Deletion of the C-term sequence 163-179 in CIDEA completely eliminates LD localization in most cells.
source: Furthermore, the deletion of this C-term sequence in CIDEA-△(163–179)-v5 completely eliminated LD localization in most of the cells (Figure 2B,C), confirming its role in LD targeting.
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The cationic amphipathic helix in the C-term participates in the TAG transference step of CIDEA activity.
source: In addition to its role in LD targeting, our data indicate that the cationic amphipathic helix in the C-term participates in the TAG transference step of CIDEA activity, as the charge inversion (K167E/R171E/R175E) did not affect LD targeting but completely blocked LD enlargement (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis and phenotypic characterization in Figure 2C.

claim: K167 in the amphipathic helix is 100% conserved across all vertebrate species examined.
source: K167 is 100% conserved across all vertebrate species examined.
evidence: This is shown through sequence alignment analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: R171 in the amphipathic helix is conserved across vertebrates including birds, snakes, lizards, crocodiles, turtles, marsupials, placental mammals, and monotremes, although not in fish.
source: R171 was conserved across vertebrates including birds, snakes, lizards, crocodiles, turtles, marsupials, placental mammals, and monotremes, although not in fish.
evidence: This is shown through sequence alignment analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An amphipathic helix is predicted in CIDEA of all vertebrate species examined.
source: Remarkably, an amphipathic helix is predicted in CIDEA of all the vertebrate species examined (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown through computational structure prediction across species in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absence of negative charges in the helix is an essential condition to permit TAG transference.
source: The absence of negative charges in the helix appeared to be an essential condition to permit TAG transference, as a single inverted charge mutation such as R171E or R175E was sufficient to block LD enlargement (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Conservative substitutions such as R171K or K167R do not affect CIDEA activity.
source: In contrast, conservative substitutions such as R171K or K167R did not affect CIDEA activity, and even the substitution of the three basic aas with histidine in (K167H/R171H/R175H)-CIDEA-v5 was compatible with the formation of large LDs, strongly supporting the conclusion from sequence comparison that positive charges are required at these positions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletions in the N-term domain of CIDEA impair LD-LD docking.
source: Deletions in the N-term domain of CIDEA impaired LD–LD docking, as shown by the increase in cells displaying isolated LDs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: LD clustering can be induced by forcing the LD localization of the N-term fragment through conjugation with the 18-aa amphipathic helix.
source: Furthermore, LD clustering could be induced by forcing the LD localization of the N-term fragment through conjugation with the 18-aa amphipathic helix (HA-CIDEA-(1–117)-(162–180)) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3D (note: text says 3C but refers to Figure 3D).

claim: The C-term fragment (116-217) of CIDEA retains some degree of LD-LD docking activity.
source: However, the C-term fragment (116–217) retained some degree of LD–LD docking activity (Figure 2C), indicating that an additional interaction site could be present in this region.
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Complete blocking of LD clustering is observed with the CIDEA fragment 152-217, which lacks the N-term and a section of the C-term.
source: In fact, a complete blocking of LD clustering was only observed with the shorter fragment 152–217, which lacks the N-term and a section of the C-term (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4A.

claim: The formation of CIDEA-CIDEA complexes was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation of CIDEA-v5 with CIDEA-HA.
source: The formation of CIDEA–CIDEA complexes was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of CIDEA-v5 with CIDEA-HA.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-IP of CIDEA was observed with CIDEA-(116-217)-v5 but not CIDEA-(1-118)-v5, indicating that the C-term is responsible for that interaction.
source: Surprisingly, co-IP was observed with CIDEA-(116–217)-v5 but not CIDEA-(1–118)-v5, indicating that the C-term was responsible for that interaction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4B.

claim: Within the C-term region, the deletion of the 162-197 sequence does not affect co-IP whereas the signal is largely reduced in CIDEA-△(126-155)-v5.
source: Within the C-term region, the deletion of the 162–197 sequence did not affect the co-IP whereas the signal was largely reduced in CIDEA-△(126–155)-v5 (Figure 4B), indicating that this conserved region was involved in the C-term interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4B.

claim: The equivalent mutations in CIDEA (E79Q/D80N and R47E) to those that disrupt N-term dimerization in CIDEC impair LD docking.
source: Interestingly, we found that the equivalent mutations in CIDEA (E79Q/D80N and R47E) impaired LD docking, while R47Q and R47A, which would not create repulsions between the interacting domains, did not affect CIDEA activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis and phenotypic characterization in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the C-term dimerization site (126-155) and the N-term domain of CIDEA can contribute to LD-LD docking by forming complexes with their counterparts on the adjacent LD.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both the C-term dimerization site (126–155) and the N-term domain of CIDEA can contribute to LD–LD docking by forming complexes with its counterparts on the adjacent LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP and mutational analysis data.

claim: The N-term of CIDEC is involved in LD-LD docking, as its deletion increases the fraction of cells displaying isolated LDs.
source: Here we show that similar to CIDEA, the N-term of CIDEC is involved in LD–LD docking, as its deletion increases the fraction of cells displaying isolated LDs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The C-term of CIDEC is sufficient for docking and enlarging LDs in cells where it can effectively induce LD-LD docking.
source: However, in the cells where the C-term of CIDEC could effectively induce LD–LD docking, large LDs were observed instead of LD clusters, showing that although its docking efficiency is reduced, this region of CIDEC is sufficient for docking and enlarging the LDs.
evidence: This is shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: PLIN1 interacts with CIDEC but not CIDEA and potentiates CIDEC activity.
source: While PLIN1 interacts with CIDEC, but not CIDEA, and potentiates its activity (Sun et al., 2013; Grahn et al., 2013), we have observed that CIDEA interacts with PLIN5 (Figure 4D), which is rich in BAT (Harms and Seale, 2013; Zhou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature and confirmed through co-IP experiments in Figure 4D.

claim: CIDEA interacts with PLIN5.
source: While PLIN1 interacts with CIDEC, but not CIDEA, and potentiates its activity (Sun et al., 2013; Grahn et al., 2013), we have observed that CIDEA interacts with PLIN5 (Figure 4D), which is rich in BAT (Harms and Seale, 2013; Zhou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4D.

claim: CIDEA shows high affinity for both CIDEB and CIDEC.
source: In addition to PLIN5, CIDEA showed high affinity for both CIDEB and CIDEC, while it did not co-IP with DFF40 or DFF45, which share homology with the N-term domain of CIDE proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: CIDEA does not co-IP with DFF40 or DFF45.
source: In addition to PLIN5, CIDEA showed high affinity for both CIDEB and CIDEC, while it did not co-IP with DFF40 or DFF45, which share homology with the N-term domain of CIDE proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-IP experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: CIDEA selectively binds a set of anionic phospholipids.
source: To further characterize the interaction of CIDEA with the LD membrane, we utilized lipid strips to investigate the affinity of CIDEA for different lipids present in mammalian cell membranes and found that it selectively bound a set of anionic phospholipids (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through lipid strip assays in Figure 5A.

claim: CIDEA binds phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: PA binding was confirmed by the strong affinity of CIDEA-v5 for PA beads (Figure 5B), which was greatly reduced by pre-incubation of the lysate with soluble PA, but not phosphatidylcholine (PC).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The main PA-binding site of CIDEA is in the C-term region containing the amphipathic helix (163-180).
source: Although the N-term fragment showed some residual affinity, the main PA-binding site of CIDEA was in the C-term region containing the amphipathic helix (163–180) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays with different CIDEA constructs in Figure 5C.

claim: The charge inversion of the three cationic amino acids in the amphipathic helix results in loss of affinity for PA beads in the inactive mutant (K167E/R171E/R175E)-CIDEA-v5 without affecting its LD localization.
source: The charge inversion of its three cationic amino acids resulted in the loss of affinity for PA beads in the inactive mutant (K167E/R171E/R175E)-CIDEA-v5 without affecting its LD localization (Figure 5C), linking PA binding with the TAG-transference step (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays and immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The presence of DLPC liposomes stabilizes a sharp increase in α-helical structure (up to 40%) in the wild type CIDEA peptide.
source: The presence of DLPC liposomes stabilized a sharp increase in α-helical structure (up to 40%) and an equivalent reduction of sheet content (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), yielding higher helical content than that observed in n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside micelles (~25%, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy experiments in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The induction of helix formation by DLPC is not observed in a mutant peptide carrying the substitutions F166R/V169R/L170R.
source: In contrast, the induction of helix formation by DLPC was not observed in a mutant peptide carrying the substitutions impairing LD targeting in CIDEA-(F166R/V169R/L170R)-v5 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy experiments in Figure 5E.

claim: Both the wild type and F166R/V169R/L170R mutant peptides show significant helical content in the presence of DLPC:DLPA (9:1) vesicles.
source: Interestingly, fitting of the CD data indicated significant helical content for both the wt and mutant peptides in the presence of DLPC:DLPA (9:1) vesicles (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy experiments in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction with the negatively charged phospholipid PA can compensate for the excess of positive charges in CIDEA-(F166R/V169R/L170R)-v5.
source: This indicates that the interaction with the negatively charged phospholipid PA can compensate for the excess of positive charges in CIDEA-(F166R/V169R/L170R)-v5.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD spectroscopy data showing helix formation in the presence of PA.

claim: The wild type (163-180) helix diffuses towards the LD and penetrates into the hydrophobic region of the phospholipid monolayer covering the TAG core in CG-MD simulations.
source: The wt (163–180) helix (CTSFKAVLRNLLRFMSYA) diffused towards the LD containing 400 palmitoyl-oleoyl-glycero-phosphocholine (POPC) and 200 TAG molecules where it interacted at its full length with the LD surface and penetrated into the hydrophobic region of the phospholipid monolayer covering the TAG core (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: The charge-inverted mutant K167E/R171E/R175E shows similar LD binding behavior to wild type in CG-MD simulations.
source: A similar behaviour was observed by the charge-inverted mutant K167E/R171E/R175E (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), supporting the experimental result that these mutations do not affect LD localization in CIDEA (Figures 2C and 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No interaction with the LD is observed for the non-amphipathic F166R/L169R/V169R mutant in CG-MD simulations.
source: In contrast, no interaction with the LD was observed with the non-amphipathic F166R/L169R/V169R (Figure 5G), which also impairs LD binding in CIDEA (Figures 2C and 3E) and which was unable to attain stable secondary structure as evidenced by CD (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The wild type helix makes a stable complex with PA-containing LDs at even earlier simulation times than with PC-only containing LDs.
source: The wt helix made a stable complex with this LD at even earlier simulation times than with the PC-only containing LDs (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of PA permits the accommodation of the F166R/L169R/V169R helix in the LD monolayer in CG-MD simulations.
source: Interestingly, while the presence of PA permitted the accommodation of the F166R/L169R/V169R helix in the LD monolayer, it could not penetrate as deep towards the TAG core as the wt or helix.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: TAG molecules are able to escape the LD core and are integrated in the hydrophobic section of the membrane in CG-MD simulations.
source: We observed that TAG molecules were able to escape the LD core and were integrated in the hydrophobic section of the membrane (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5H.

claim: TAG infiltration into the membrane is increased after the docking of the wild type helix in CG-MD simulations.
source: This TAG infiltration was increased after the docking of the wt helix in the membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that CIDEA could promote the migration of TAG into the membrane as an intermediate state prior to the transference to the acceptor LD.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The wild type helix can attract PA molecules in its vicinity by the interaction of its cationic residues with the negatively charged polar head of PA in CG-MD simulations.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the wt helix could attract PA molecules in its vicinity by the interaction of its cationic residues with the negatively charged polar head of PA (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The anionic amphipathic mutant K167E/R171E/R175E is docked in a PA-depleted area and avoids PA molecules in CG-MD simulations.
source: Remarkably, CG-MD simulations showed that whereas the non-amphipathic cationic helix F166R/L169R/V169R also interacted with PA molecules from its superficial docking position in the LD membrane, the anionic amphipathic mutant K167E/R171E/R175E was docked in a PA-depleted area and avoided the PA molecules (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CG-MD simulations shown in Figure 5H.

claim: PA binding is a feature common to all three members of the CIDE protein family.
source: We found that PA binding was a feature common to all three members of the CIDE protein family (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays in Figure 5C.

claim: An inactive CIDEC identified in a patient with lipodystrophy contains a truncation (E186X) in the predicted PA-binding site.
source: Intriguingly, we determined that an inactive CIDEC identified in a patient with lipodystrophy (Rubio-Cabezas et al., 2009) contained a truncation (E186X) in the predicted PA-binding site.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of a previously reported lipodystrophy-associated mutation.

claim: hCIDEC-(E186X)-v5 is localized in LDs in a high percentage of cells but is completely unable to induce LD enlargement.
source: Although hCIDEC-(E186X)-v5 and the equivalent mCIDEA-(N172X)-v5 were localized in LDs in a high percentage of cells, they were completely unable to induce LD enlargement (Figures 2C and 5I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging and phenotypic analysis in Figures 2C and 5I.

claim: hCIDEC-(E186X)-v5 shows no affinity for PA.
source: LD clustering activity and its ability to interact with CIDE proteins was not altered in hCIDEC-(E186X)-v5 (Figure 5I, J), but it showed no affinity for PA (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays in Figure 5K.

claim: Murine CIDEA can be stably expressed in yeast cells.
source: Murine CIDEA could be stably expressed in yeast cells (Figure 6B), producing an increase in the size of their LDs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot and microscopy analysis in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Yeast cells expressing wild type CIDEA contain fewer and larger LDs than control cells.
source: Yeast cells expressing wt CIDEA, but not the inactive R171E/R175E mutant, contained fewer and larger LDs than the control (Figure 6D–F), indicating that murine CIDEA was functional in these cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy analysis and quantification in Figure 6D-F.

claim: CIDEA is inactive in yeast cells defective in phospholipase D (pld1△).
source: CIDEA was inactive in cells defective in phospholipase D (pld1△) (Rose et al., 1995), which catalyzes the production of PA from PC.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of CIDEA activity in different yeast strains in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: CIDEA activity is abrogated in yeast cells expressing a hyperactive form of PA phosphohydrolase (PAH1-7A).
source: CIDEA activity was also abrogated in cells expressing a hyperactive form of the PA phosphohydrolase (PAH1-7A) (Choi et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of CIDEA activity in different yeast strains in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Total cellular PA levels are increased by CIDEA expression in yeast.
source: In addition, we observed that total cellular PA levels were increased by CIDEA, an effect that was prevented by the expression of PAH1-7A (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phospholipid quantification in Figure 6G.

claim: The PA synthesis rate is not affected by CIDEA expression in yeast.
source: As the PA synthesis rate was not affected (Figure 6H), CIDEA could be protecting a pool of PA from degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through pulse labeling experiments in Figure 6H.

claim: CIDEA is unable to promote LD enlargement in mammalian cells expressing LIPIN-1γ-v5.
source: While CIDEA-HA displayed normal activity in cells co-transfected with an empty vector, it was unable to promote LD enlargement in cells expressing LIPIN-1γ-v5 (Figure 6I, J).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence imaging and phenotypic analysis in Figure 6I and 6J.

claim: LIPIN-1γ-v5 shows affinity for PA but does not co-IP with CIDEA.
source: LIPIN-1γ-v5 showed affinity for PA but it did not co-IP with CIDEA, indicating that its inhibitory effects were not due to a direct interaction between these proteins (Figure 6K, L).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PA bead binding assays and co-IP experiments in Figure 6K and 6L.

claim: The mechanism of action of CIDEA involves direct interaction with PA molecules in the LD monolayer.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that the mechanism of action of CIDEA involves direct interaction with PA molecules in the LD monolayer.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined results of PA binding assays, PA depletion experiments, and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The Cidea gene is highly expressed in BAT.
source: The Cidea gene is highly expressed in BAT, induced in WAT following cold exposure (Rosell et al., 2014), and is widely used by researchers as a defining marker to discriminate brown or brite adipocytes from white adipocytes (Harms and Seale, 2013; Zhou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Cidea is induced in WAT following cold exposure.
source: The Cidea gene is highly expressed in BAT, induced in WAT following cold exposure (Rosell et al., 2014), and is widely used by researchers as a defining marker to discriminate brown or brite adipocytes from white adipocytes (Harms and Seale, 2013; Zhou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Cidea is widely used as a defining marker to discriminate brown or brite adipocytes from white adipocytes.
source: The Cidea gene is highly expressed in BAT, induced in WAT following cold exposure (Rosell et al., 2014), and is widely used by researchers as a defining marker to discriminate brown or brite adipocytes from white adipocytes (Harms and Seale, 2013; Zhou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The full process of LD enlargement can be induced in yeast by the sole exogenous expression of CIDEA.
source: In spite of this, the full process of LD enlargement can be induced in yeast by the sole exogenous expression of CIDEA, indicating that in contrast to SNARE-triggered vesicle fusion, LD fusion by lipid transference does not require the coordination of multiple specific proteins (Risselada and Grubmuller, 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated through yeast experiments in Figure 6.

claim: LD fusion by lipid transference does not require the coordination of multiple specific proteins, in contrast to SNARE-triggered vesicle fusion.
source: In spite of this, the full process of LD enlargement can be induced in yeast by the sole exogenous expression of CIDEA, indicating that in contrast to SNARE-triggered vesicle fusion, LD fusion by lipid transference does not require the coordination of multiple specific proteins (Risselada and Grubmuller, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of CIDEA alone to induce LD fusion in yeast.

claim: LD fusion is a spontaneous process that the cell has to prevent by tightly controlling phospholipid composition.
source: While vesicle fusion implies an intricate restructuring of the phospholipid bilayers, LD fusion is a spontaneous process that the cell has to prevent by tightly controlling their phospholipid composition (Krahmer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature and general knowledge of LD biology.

claim: Complete LD fusion by lipid transfer can last several hours.
source: Complete LD fusion by lipid transfer can last several hours, during which the participating LDs remain in contact.
evidence: This is observed through time-lapse microscopy experiments shown in Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 1.

claim: Although LDs can be tightly packed in cultured adipocytes, no TAG transference across neighbour LDs is observed in the absence of CIDE proteins.
source: In fact, although LDs can be tightly packed in cultured adipocytes, no TAG transference across neighbour LDs is observed in the absence of CIDE proteins (Gong et al., 2011), showing that the phospholipid monolayer acts as a barrier impermeable to TAG.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The phospholipid monolayer acts as a barrier impermeable to TAG.
source: In fact, although LDs can be tightly packed in cultured adipocytes, no TAG transference across neighbour LDs is observed in the absence of CIDE proteins (Gong et al., 2011), showing that the phospholipid monolayer acts as a barrier impermeable to TAG.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LD fusion does not occur without CIDE proteins.

claim: PA is a cone-shaped anionic phospholipid that could locally destabilize the LD monolayer by favouring a negative membrane curvature.
source: PA, whose requirement is indicated by our PA-depletion experiments, is a cone-shaped anionic phospholipid that could locally destabilize the LD monolayer by favouring a negative membrane curvature that is incompatible with the spherical LD morphology (Kooijman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature and the physical properties of PA.

claim: The zwitterion PC, the main component of the LD monolayer, stabilizes the LD structure.
source: Interestingly, while the zwitterion PC, the main component of the monolayer, stabilizes the LD structure (Krahmer et al., 2011), the negatively charged PA promotes their coalescence (Fei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The negatively charged PA promotes LD coalescence.
source: Interestingly, while the zwitterion PC, the main component of the monolayer, stabilizes the LD structure (Krahmer et al., 2011), the negatively charged PA promotes their coalescence (Fei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: During LD fusion by lipid transfer, the pressure gradient experienced by LDs favours TAG flux from small to large LDs.
source: During LD fusion by lipid transfer, the pressure gradient experienced by LDs favours TAG flux from small to large LDs (Gong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Cidea mRNA is the LD protein-encoding transcript that experiences the greatest increase during the cold-induced process by which multilocular BAT-like cells appear in WAT.
source: Interestingly, Cidea mRNA is the LD protein-encoding transcript that experiences the greatest increase during the cold-induced process by which multilocular BAT-like cells appear in WAT (Barneda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: In BAT, cold exposure instigates a profound increase in CIDEA protein levels that is independent of transcriptional regulation.
source: Furthermore, in BAT, cold exposure instigates a profound increase in CIDEA protein levels that is independent of transcriptional regulation (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The profound increase in CIDEA is coincident with elevated lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis that occurs in both brown and white adipose tissues after β-adrenergic receptor activation.
source: The profound increase in CIDEA is coincident with elevated lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis that occurs in both brown and white adipose tissues after β-adrenergic receptor activation (Mottillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: CIDEA has a central role in coupling lipolysis and lipogenesis to package newly synthesized TAG in LDs for subsequent lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation.
source: It is likely that CIDEA has a central role in coupling these processes to package newly synthesized TAG in LDs for subsequent lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the coincidence of CIDEA increase with elevated lipolysis and lipogenesis.

claim: BAT displays high levels of glycerol kinase activity that facilitates glycerol recycling rather than release into the blood stream.
source: Importantly, BAT displays high levels of glycerol kinase activity (Bertin, 1976; Bertin et al., 1984) that facilitates glycerol recycling rather than release into the blood stream, following induction of lipolysis (Portet et al., 1974), which occurs in WAT.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The elevated glycerol released from cells depleted of CIDEA is likely a result of decoupling lipolysis from the ability to efficiently store the products of lipogenesis in LDs.
source: Hence, the reported elevated glycerol released from cells depleted of CIDEA (Zhou et al., 2003) is likely to be a result of decoupling lipolysis from the ability to efficiently store the products of lipogenesis in LDs, therefore producing a net increase in detected extracellular glycerol.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of CIDEA in LD enlargement and the glycerol recycling capacity of BAT.

claim: CIDEA-dependent LD enlargement is maintained in a lipase-negative yeast strain.
source: This important role of CIDEA is supported by the marked depletion of TAG in the BAT of Cidea-null mice following overnight exposure to a temperature of 4°C (Zhou et al., 2003) and by our finding that CIDEA-dependent LD enlargement is maintained in a lipase-negative yeast strain.
evidence: This is demonstrated through yeast experiments in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Cidea and genes required to facilitate high rates of lipolysis and lipogenesis are associated with the 'browning' of white fat.
source: Cidea and the genes that are required to facilitate high rates of lipolysis and lipogenesis are associated with the 'browning' of white fat either following cold exposure (Rosell et al., 2014) or in genetic models such as RIP140 knockout WAT (Kiskinis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: The induction of a brown-like phenotype in WAT has potential benefits in the treatment and prevention of metabolic disorders.
source: The induction of a brown-like phenotype in WAT has potential benefits in the treatment and prevention of metabolic disorders (Whittle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of large LDs has been observed in non-adipocyte cells under pathological conditions such as liver steatosis and atherosclerosis.
source: Abnormal accumulation of large LDs have also been observed in non-adipocyte cells under other pathological conditions such as liver steatosis and atherosclerosis (Krahmer and Walther, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Enhanced expression of CIDE proteins has been linked to liver steatosis and atherosclerosis.
source: As enhanced expression of CIDE proteins have been linked to these conditions (Li et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2012; Matsusue et al., 2008), the modulation of CIDE-triggered LD enlargement represents a potential therapeutic strategy that requires the elucidation of its molecular mechanism.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: During LD fusion by lipid transference, CIDEA ensures the close proximity of the LD membranes by forming trans complexes through its N-term and C-term dimerization sites.
source: In summary, we found that during LD fusion by lipid transference, CIDEA ensures the close proximity of the LD membranes by forming trans complexes through its N-term and C-term dimerization sites.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the co-IP and mutational analysis data presented.

claim: The CIDEA protein complex is anchored in the LD-LD interface, forming the molecular environment necessary for TAG transport across the membrane.
source: This protein complex will be anchored in the LD–LD interface, forming the molecular environment necessary for TAG transport across the membrane.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The amphipathic helix embedded in the LD membrane interacts with the cone-shaped phospholipid PA, generating a local perturbation of the monolayer integrity that increases its permeability to TAG.
source: Finally, the amphipathic helix embedded in the LD membrane interacts with the cone-shaped phospholipid PA, generating a local perturbation of the monolayer integrity that would increase its permeability to TAG and enable its exportation to the acceptor LD.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PA binding, CD spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulation data.
